result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch14-data-to-decision-capstone status: complete --- # Data-to-decision capstone {#sec-data-to-decision-capstone} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: This capstone follows one analysis from a committed data file to a conditional intervention comparison. The point is not to make a historical claim from a small table. It is to make every transition visible: provenance, model choice, fitting, diagnostics, uncertainty, sensitivity, and a decision-relevant scenario. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - load and verify a versioned local dataset without a render-time download; - distinguish observations from reconstructed latent SIR states; - fit a small ODE model with bounded `Optimization.jl` parameters; - diagnose fit mismatch and summarize deterministic parameter uncertainty; - propagate parameter changes through a sensitivity calculation; and - compare an intervention scenario with a fitted-rate reference trajectory. ## Model assumptions and classification The data are the eight committed Eyam observations described in [`data/README.md`](../data/README.md). The versioned [dataset](../data/eyam_plague_1666.csv) and its [provenance metadata](../data/eyam_plague_1666.toml) are both in the course repository. They cover the second wave beginning on 18 June 1666, with a modeled population of 261. The historical context is discussed by Raggett (@raggett1982) and by the later epidemiological analysis of Whittles and Didelot (@whittles2016). We choose a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, homogeneous closed SIR model because it is the smallest model that connects the three columns and the preceding course units. This is a deliberately limited model choice. The `S` and `I` values are **reconstructed from historical records and model assumptions, not direct measurements**. A homogeneous closed SIR model also omits important plague mechanisms, including rodent-to-human transmission, household structure, population movement, and changing reporting. The modeled population is the population at the start of the second wave, not the pre-plague village population. ## Equations For this small dataset we fit an effective transmission rate $\lambda=\beta c$ and a recovery/removal rate $\gamma$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -\lambda\frac{SI}{N},\\ \frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= \lambda\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\\ \frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= \gamma I. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-capstone-sir} The initial state is fixed to the first row, and the fitted trajectory is compared with all three reconstructed state columns. For an intervention scenario we add cumulative incidence $C$ and multiply $\lambda$ by $1-v(t)$: $$ \frac{\mathrm dC}{\mathrm dt} = (1-v(t))\lambda\frac{SI}{N}. $$ {#eq-capstone-intervention} The least-squares objective is $$ L(\lambda,\gamma)= \sum_{k=1}^{8}\sum_{j\in\{S,I,R\}} \left(\frac{x_j(t_k;\lambda,\gamma)-x_{j,k}}{N}\right)^2. $$ {#eq-capstone-loss} This is a transparent teaching objective, not a claim that historical counts have Gaussian errors. A count likelihood, reporting model, or mechanistic plague model would be appropriate for a substantive historical analysis. The three residual series are not independent. Both the data and the model conserve the population, so at every observation time $$ e_S(t_k)+e_I(t_k)+e_R(t_k)=0, \qquad e_j(t_k)=x_j(t_k;\lambda,\gamma)-x_{j,k}. $$ {#eq-capstone-residual-constraint} Fitting all three states is therefore an equal-weighted redundant criterion rather than three independent sources of information: only two of the three residuals can be chosen freely. The objective remains usable as a teaching criterion, but it should not be read as three times the evidence of a single-state fit. ## Julia implementation The data path is local and there is no fallback: a capstone about provenance must not silently substitute anything for the committed file. If the CSV is missing or its bytes do not match the recorded digest, the render fails here rather than producing a clean figure of something else. No code in this chapter fetches epidemiological data from the network. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using CSV using DataFrames using DiffEqCallbacks using OrdinaryDiffEq using Optimization using OptimizationOptimJL using SHA using TOML course_root = normpath(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..")) include(joinpath(course_root, "src", "EpiModelingCourse.jl")) using .EpiModelingCourse data_path = joinpath(course_root, "data", "eyam_plague_1666.csv") metadata_path = joinpath(course_root, "data", "eyam_plague_1666.toml") metadata = TOML.parsefile(metadata_path) population = Float64(metadata["population"]) observation_columns = [:time_months, :S, :I, :R] @assert isfile(data_path) "Committed Eyam dataset is missing: $(data_path)" actual_checksum = bytes2hex(sha256(read(data_path))) @assert actual_checksum == metadata["csv_sha256"] data = CSV.read(data_path, DataFrame) data_source = "committed Eyam CSV, SHA-256 verified" @assert String.(names(data)) == String.(observation_columns) @assert nrow(data) == 8 @assert all(diff(data.time_months) .> 0) @assert all(isapprox.(data.S .+ data.I .+ data.R, population; atol = 1e-8)) ``` ::: The metadata records the expected SHA-256 digest, the packaged MultiBD source, and the Apache 2.0 license. A checksum verifies that this checkout contains the committed bytes; it does not prove that the historical reconstruction is correct. Provenance and interpretation caveats remain part of the model decision. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} data_source, metadata["provenance"], metadata["interpretation"]["caveats"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ("committed Eyam CSV, SHA-256 verified", Dict{String, Any}("primary_record" => "Burial register of St. Lawrence Church, Eyam, Derbyshire", "analytical_source" => "Raggett, G. F. (1982), A stochastic model of the Eyam plague", "packaged_source_url" => "https://github.com/msuchard/MultiBD", "analytical_source_doi" => "10.1080/02664768200000021", "packaged_source_file" => "R/Eyam.R and data/Eyam.rda", "packaged_source_file_sha" => "1f0947c3777216360e8eeb16c774ebe7109a9b57", "packaged_source" => "MultiBD 1.0.2", "packaged_source_license" => "Apache License 2.0"), ["The population of 261 is the population at the start of the second wave, not the pre-plague village population.", "The S and I series are model-derived reconstructions from historical records rather than direct measurements.", "A simple closed homogeneous SIR model omits possible rodent-to-human transmission and population movement.", "The final observation is one month after the preceding observation; earlier intervals are half a month."]) ``` ::: ::: ### Fitting the effective SIR model The fitting kernel is written out in full below. Its `λ` parameter is an effective rate; it should not be reported as a separately identified contact rate and transmission probability. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} observation_times = Float64.(data.time_months) initial_state = Float64.(collect(data[1, [:S, :I, :R]])) observed_states = permutedims(Matrix{Float64}(data[:, [:S, :I, :R]])) function fit_rhs!(du, u, p, t) λ, γ = p S, I, R = u incidence = λ * S * I / population du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I return nothing end function fit_loss(θ, _) problem = ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), θ, ) solution = solve( problem, Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8, ) prediction = Array(solution) return sum(((prediction .- observed_states) ./ population) .^ 2) end coarse_grid = [ (fit_loss([λ, γ], nothing), λ, γ) for λ in range(0.5, 6.0; length = 15) for γ in range(0.5, 4.0; length = 15) ] grid_start = coarse_grid[argmin(first.(coarse_grid))] fit_objective = OptimizationFunction(fit_loss, AutoFiniteDiff()) fit_problem = OptimizationProblem( fit_objective, [grid_start[2], grid_start[3]], nothing; lb = [1e-4, 1e-4], ub = [8.0, 8.0], ) fit_solution = solve(fit_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 60) fitted_parameters = Float64.(fit_solution.u) fitted_loss = fit_solution.objective fitted_parameters, fitted_loss ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ([4.603717504388643, 2.8076873724509857], 0.00390067987740599) ``` ::: ::: ### Diagnostics The model and data are shown together, followed by residuals. The residual pattern is more useful than a single loss value: systematic timing or peak mismatch is evidence that the homogeneous SIR mechanism is inadequate for the question. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fitted_solution = solve( ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), fitted_parameters, ), Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8, ) fitted_states = Array(fitted_solution) residuals = fitted_states .- observed_states state_rmse = sqrt.(vec(sum(residuals .^ 2; dims = 2)) ./ nrow(data)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 3.670787952976688 2.9810634731108814 3.294442762389717 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-fit-diagnostics .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (950, 750)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "people") state_labels = ["S", "I", "R"] state_colors = [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen] for j in 1:3 lines!(ax1, observation_times, fitted_states[j, :], color = state_colors[j], label = "$(state_labels[j]) model") scatter!(ax1, observation_times, observed_states[j, :], color = state_colors[j], markersize = 9, label = "$(state_labels[j]) data") end axislegend(ax1, position = :rb, nbanks = 2) ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "model − data") for j in 1:3 lines!(ax2, observation_times, residuals[j, :], color = state_colors[j], label = state_labels[j]) end hlines!(ax2, [0.0], color = :black, linestyle = :dash) axislegend(ax2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-fit-diagnostics .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Fitted homogeneous SIR states and residuals for the committed Eyam observations. ::: ::: ### Deterministic uncertainty envelope The historical states are reconstructed and there are only eight rows, so a formal confidence interval would require an explicit observation model. As a transparent alternative, we construct a deterministic parameter envelope: the $3\times3$ combinations of $\pm10\%$ around the fitted parameters are retained when their loss is close to the best loss. This is an uncertainty scenario, not a calibrated confidence interval. The acceptance tolerance is a modeling choice, so it is worth stating in units a reader can check. @eq-capstone-loss sums $8\times3=24$ squared residuals scaled by $N$, so a total loss $L$ corresponds to a root-mean-square residual of $N\sqrt{L/24}$ people per state observation. The tolerance $0.02$ therefore admits candidates whose typical residual is about eight people rather than the fitted three — roughly a doubling of the misfit, chosen to be visible on the figure without admitting parameters the data clearly reject. Because some $\pm10\%$ candidates fail this test, the band below is an *accepted local-grid envelope*, not a $\pm10\%$ envelope; `length(accepted_parameters)` reports how many of the nine survived. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} parameter_candidates = [ fitted_parameters .* [λ_scale, γ_scale] for λ_scale in [0.9, 1.0, 1.1] for γ_scale in [0.9, 1.0, 1.1] ] accepted_parameters = [ parameters for parameters in parameter_candidates if fit_loss(parameters, nothing) <= fitted_loss + 0.02 ] accepted_predictions = [ Array(solve( ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), parameters, ), Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, )) for parameters in accepted_parameters ] infectious_lower = [minimum(prediction[2, k] for prediction in accepted_predictions) for k in eachindex(observation_times)] infectious_upper = [maximum(prediction[2, k] for prediction in accepted_predictions) for k in eachindex(observation_times)] (candidates = length(parameter_candidates), accepted = length(accepted_parameters)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (candidates = 9, accepted = 3) ``` ::: ::: The candidates that survive are the ones that scale $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ together, leaving $\lambda/\gamma$ near its fitted value; the off-diagonal combinations that change the ratio are rejected. The envelope is therefore tracing the ridge of near-equivalent fits rather than a box around the optimum, which is the same identifiability structure that the sensitivity calculation below picks up. ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-uncertainty .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (850, 450)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "infectious people") band!(ax, observation_times, infectious_lower, infectious_upper, color = (:steelblue, 0.25), label = "accepted local-grid envelope") lines!(ax, observation_times, fitted_states[2, :], color = :firebrick, label = "fitted model") scatter!(ax, observation_times, observed_states[2, :], color = :black, label = "reconstructed I") axislegend(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-uncertainty .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A deterministic accepted local-grid envelope for infectious prevalence. ::: ::: ### Sensitivity and intervention comparison For a decision-oriented output, we propagate the fitted parameters to cumulative incidence at a fixed horizon. Three things about that output need stating before it is used. First, the horizon is month 8 but the observations end at month 4, so every number below is a four-month extrapolation of a model fitted to the first four months. It is not an observed endpoint, and it is the model's cumulative incidence at month 8 rather than a guaranteed asymptotic final size — whether the two coincide is something the trajectory has to show, not something the horizon guarantees. The variable names carry the horizon for this reason. Second, $C$ is initialized at $C(0)=0$, so it counts new infections *after* the first observation and excludes the seven people already infectious at $t=0$. Since $\mathrm dC/\mathrm dt=-\mathrm dS/\mathrm dt$, it satisfies $C(t)=S(0)-S(t)$; the total ever infected is $C(t)+I(0)$. Third, the reduction is applied on top of the fitted rate. The fitted $\lambda$ was estimated from data recorded during the outbreak itself, so it already summarizes whatever conditions and actions were in force at the time. Because the fitted effective transmission rate already reflects conditions during the observed period, the reference trajectory represents no additional modeled reduction — not the historical outbreak with actual Eyam actions removed. The comparison below is between a fitted-rate reference and the same rate with an additional modeled reduction, and it is named that way throughout. The summary below reports incidence at the last observation alongside incidence at the horizon, and the infectious prevalence still remaining at the horizon, so you can see for yourself how much of the reported number was extrapolated and whether the model has actually burned out by month 8. The centered one-percent perturbation is a local sensitivity check; it is not a replacement for the broader analysis in @sec-sensitivity-and-identifiability. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function decision_rhs!(du, u, p, t) λ, γ, reduction, N = p S, I, R, C = u incidence = (1 - reduction) * λ * S * I / N du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I du[4] = incidence return nothing end function decision_solution( start_time; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5, horizon = 8.0, ) stop_time = start_time + duration @assert 0 <= reduction <= 1 "reduction must be a fraction in [0, 1]" @assert duration >= 0 "duration must be nonnegative" @assert 0 <= start_time <= horizon "start_time must lie within [0, horizon]" @assert stop_time <= horizon "the intervention must end within the horizon" parameters = [fitted_parameters[1], fitted_parameters[2], 0.0, population] problem = ODEProblem( decision_rhs!, [initial_state..., 0.0], (0.0, horizon), parameters, ) if duration <= 0.0 || reduction <= 0.0 return solve(problem, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1) end function affect!(integrator) integrator.p[3] = integrator.t < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0 return nothing end callback = PresetTimeCallback([start_time, stop_time], affect!) return solve(problem, Tsit5(); callback = callback, saveat = 0.1) end function cumulative_incidence_at_month_8(start_time; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5) return Array(decision_solution( start_time; duration = duration, reduction = reduction, ))[4, end] end function month8_incidence_for_parameters(parameters) solution = solve( ODEProblem( decision_rhs!, [initial_state..., 0.0], (0.0, 8.0), [parameters[1], parameters[2], 0.0, population], ), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1, ) return Array(solution)[4, end] end function relative_parameter_sensitivity(parameter_index) perturbation = 0.01 * fitted_parameters[parameter_index] lower = copy(fitted_parameters) upper = copy(fitted_parameters) lower[parameter_index] -= perturbation upper[parameter_index] += perturbation lower_output = month8_incidence_for_parameters(lower) upper_output = month8_incidence_for_parameters(upper) baseline_output = month8_incidence_for_parameters(fitted_parameters) return (upper_output - lower_output) / (2 * perturbation) * fitted_parameters[parameter_index] / baseline_output end relative_month8_incidence_sensitivity = [ relative_parameter_sensitivity(index) for index in 1:2 ] reference_scenario = decision_solution(0.0; duration = 0.0, reduction = 0.0) reduced_scenario = decision_solution(1.0; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5) decision_summary = ( λ = fitted_parameters[1], γ = fitted_parameters[2], month4_incidence_reference = Array(reference_scenario)[4, findfirst(≈(last(observation_times)), reference_scenario.t)], month8_incidence_reference = Array(reference_scenario)[4, end], month8_incidence_with_reduction = Array(reduced_scenario)[4, end], infectious_remaining_at_horizon = Array(reference_scenario)[2, end], relative_month8_incidence_sensitivity = relative_month8_incidence_sensitivity, ) decision_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (λ = 4.603717504388643, γ = 2.8076873724509857, month4_incidence_reference = 168.05436214142952, month8_incidence_reference = 170.942665854259, month8_incidence_with_reduction = 138.13851031114234, infectious_remaining_at_horizon = 0.012397527687108183, relative_month8_incidence_sensitivity = [1.1369942301630875, -1.1359021476043987]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-decision-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (900, 500)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months", ylabel = "cumulative incidence since month 0") decision_times = reference_scenario.t reference_array = Array(reference_scenario) reduced_array = Array(reduced_scenario(decision_times)) lines!(ax, decision_times, reference_array[4, :], color = :firebrick, label = "fitted-rate reference") lines!(ax, decision_times, reduced_array[4, :], color = :steelblue, label = "additional 50% reduction from month 1") vlines!(ax, [last(observation_times)], color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "last observation") vspan!(ax, 1.0, 2.0, color = (:steelblue, 0.15)) axislegend(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-decision-comparison .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Cumulative incidence to month 8 with and without an additional modeled reduction, relative to the fitted-rate reference. Observations end at month 4, so the curves are extrapolated beyond that point. ::: ::: ## Validation The data checks validate schema, ordering, population conservation, and the committed checksum. The model checks validate that the optimizer and every solver call actually converged — a finite number can be returned by a failed solve, so the return codes are checked rather than inferred — and then that the trajectory conserves population, stays nonnegative, and satisfies the cumulative-incidence identity $C(t)=S(0)-S(t)$. The decision comparison checks that the additional reduction lowers cumulative incidence for this fitted scenario. These are structural checks, not evidence that the model is historically adequate. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fit_conservation_error = maximum( abs.(vec(sum(fitted_states; dims = 1)) .- population), ) reference_array_check = Array(reference_scenario) cumulative_identity_error = maximum( abs.(reference_array_check[4, :] .- (initial_state[1] .- reference_array_check[1, :])), ) policy_reduction = Array(reference_scenario)[4, end] - Array(reduced_scenario)[4, end] @assert SciMLBase.successful_retcode(fit_solution.retcode) @assert SciMLBase.successful_retcode(fitted_solution.retcode) @assert SciMLBase.successful_retcode(reference_scenario.retcode) @assert SciMLBase.successful_retcode(reduced_scenario.retcode) @assert all(isfinite, fitted_parameters) && isfinite(fitted_loss) @assert all(isfinite, fitted_states) @assert all(>=(-1e-8), fitted_states) @assert all(>=(-1e-8), reference_array_check) @assert fit_conservation_error < 1e-6 @assert cumulative_identity_error < 1e-6 @assert policy_reduction > 0 (source = data_source, fit_conservation_error = fit_conservation_error, cumulative_identity_error = cumulative_identity_error, state_rmse = state_rmse, policy_reduction = policy_reduction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (source = "committed Eyam CSV, SHA-256 verified", fit_conservation_error = 5.684341886080802e-14, cumulative_identity_error = 5.684341886080802e-14, state_rmse = [3.670787952976688, 2.9810634731108814, 3.294442762389717], policy_reduction = 32.80415554311665) ``` ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The fitted $\lambda$ summarizes transmission under the data's time scale; it does not identify separate $\beta$ and $c$. The deterministic envelope captures only a deliberately narrow local perturbation and the residual diagnostic shows why uncertainty should not be reduced to optimizer digits. The intervention comparison is made under the same homogeneous closed SIR assumptions, and its reference arm deserves care. The fitted $\lambda$ is an *effective* rate estimated from the outbreak as it actually unfolded, so the conditions and actions in force during those four months are already baked into it. The reference trajectory is therefore a constant-$\lambda$ scenario with no additional modeled reduction; it is not Eyam with its historical actions stripped out, and the gap between the two curves is not the effect of the village's real response. Both arms also run four months past the last observation. Because `S` and `I` are reconstructed values and a homogeneous closed SIR omits important plague mechanisms, the result is an educational model-based comparison, not a historical estimate of the effect of a specific Eyam action. Replacing the model with a household, vector-borne, movement, or observation model would change both the fit and the decision. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch14-ex1} Replace the state least-squares loss with a loss on `I` only, refit $(\lambda,\gamma)$, and compare the residual plot and the implied cumulative incidence $S(0)-S(t_8)$ over the observation window with the all-state fit. Explain which information is discarded and why a seemingly better infectious curve may fit the reconstructed $S$ and $R$ series worse, even though both fitted trajectories conserve $S+I+R=N$. ### Exercise 2 {#ch14-ex2} Use the deterministic envelope to compare a one-month 25% reduction with a one-month 50% reduction beginning at month 1. Report the range of cumulative incidence at month 8 across accepted parameter candidates for each scenario, then state what additional observation or mechanistic assumption would be needed before treating that range as decision uncertainty. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/14-data-to-decision-capstone.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/14-data-to-decision-capstone.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/14-data-to-decision-capstone.jl)
